 765-KV TRANSMISSION LINE PROJECT IN                 §
 BELL, BURNET, CONCHO, CORYELL,                      §
 LAMPASAS,       LLANO,      MASON,                  §
 MCCULLOCH, MENARD, MILAM, MILLS,                    §
 SAN SABA, SCHLEICHER, TOM GREEN,                    §
 AND WILLIAMSON COUNTIES                             §

                 FLEMING SPRINGS RANCH LAND COMPANY, LLC’S
                                REPLY BRIEF

TO THE HONORABLE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES:

       Intervenor Fleming Springs Ranch Land Company, LLC (“Fleming Springs”) files this

Reply Brief and respectfully shows:

       The majority of Intervenors who filed initial briefs, including Fleming Springs, support

either Route 894 or Route 487. A number of Intervenors who filed initial briefs support Routes

296 and 891. Fleming Springs would not oppose Routes 296 and 891. Fleming Springs would

also not oppose a number of the “RFI Routes,” including Route Cherokee Creek G (“CCG”) which

is supported by another group of intervenors.

       Fleming Springs explained in its Initial Brief the reasons it believes Route 392 under-

performs relative to Route 894 and stands by that analysis. A few more specific responses follow.

       The Brady Creek Intervenor’s (“BCI”) case, as briefed, focuses on a single question: where

should the proposed transmission line cross the Colorado River. Fleming Springs does not dispute

that the Colorado River crossing is a significant component of the project. However, the proposed

transmission line extends approximately 220 miles across fifteen Texas counties. While BCI may

FLEMING SPRINGS REPLY BRIEF                                                              PAGE 1
 want to focus on the crossing of the Colorado River, the Commission will have to balance all

aspects of the proposed route.

        The keystone to BCI’s argument is the fact that Link U3 parallels an existing line where it

crosses the Colorado. BCI asserts that this paralleling would prevent “introducing an entirely new

above-ground disturbance across the Colorado.” BCI Initial Brief, p. 7. As Fleming Springs

explained in its Initial Brief, this claimed benefit – the traditional benefit of parallelling – is absent

here. The transmission line at issue in this Docket, wherever it is built, will dwarf any existing

structures. The girth of its right-of-way will eclipse any paralleled right-of-way. To claim any

ecological advantage from U3’s transmission line parallelling would be to ignore the enormity of

the project being contemplated. U3’s paralleling is false parallelling.

        On nearly every other metric besides paralleling existing transmission lines, Route 894

performs as well or better than Route 392. BCI’s brief does not seriously engage with this EA data.

The Commission is required to weigh all of the applicable criteria across the entire study area, and

when it does, the record supports Route 894. BCI’s singular focus on Link U3’s paralleling of an

existing transmission line at the Colorado crossing does not carry the weight they ask it to bear.
